title: Accessibility (a11y)
blurb: Semantic HTML first, ARIA second, keyboard always. What WCAG actually asks of a CRUD app, and the accessibility bugs interviewers expect a mid-level developer to catch in review.

questions.q: WCAG groups its success criteria under four principles, known as POUR. What do the letters stand for?
choices: Presentable, Operable, Usable, Readable
Perceivable, Organised, Usable, Responsive
Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust
Predictable, Operable, Understandable, Reliable
questions.why: Perceivable (you can sense it: alt text, captions, contrast), Operable (you can use it: keyboard, enough time), Understandable (clear labels and errors) and Robust (works with assistive technology through valid semantics). "Predictable" is a guideline inside Understandable, not a principle.
questions.asked: A warm-up; a strong candidate maps each letter to a concrete bug they have fixed, such as a missing label under Perceivable or a mouse-only control under Operable.

questions.q: Which WCAG conformance level do most accessibility laws and procurement standards require?
choices: Level AA, which also includes every Level A criterion
Level A only, because AA and AAA are optional extras
Level AAA, because anything lower counts as failing
Level AA for text content and Level A for form controls
questions.why: Levels are cumulative: AA conformance means meeting all A and AA criteria. Section 508, EN 301 549 (used by the European Accessibility Act) and the 2024 ADA Title II rule all point at AA. AAA is not expected for whole sites, because some of its criteria cannot be met for all content.
questions.asked: Checks you know the realistic target for a CRUD app, and a good answer adds who benefits: keyboard users, screen reader users, low-vision users and people with cognitive disabilities.

questions.q: What is the first rule of ARIA use?
choices: Add a `role` to every interactive element so assistive technology can always identify it
If a native element has the semantics and behaviour you need, use it instead of ARIA
Prefer ARIA roles to native elements, because roles are announced more consistently
Only put ARIA attributes on content that is hidden from sighted users
questions.why: A native `<button>`, `<a href>` or `<select>` brings its role, focusability, keyboard handling and state for free; ARIA only changes what is announced. Adding `role="button"` to a real `<button>` is redundant, and adding it to a `<div>` promises behaviour you now have to build by hand.
questions.asked: Interviewers use it to see whether you reach for ARIA as a patch or understand that no ARIA is better than bad ARIA.

questions.q: In code review you see this "button". What happens for a keyboard-only user?
choices: Tab reaches it, but Enter does nothing until you add a keydown handler
It works with Enter, but screen readers announce it as plain text
It works for everyone except screen reader users, who hear no role
Tab never reaches it, so they cannot focus or activate it at all
questions.why: A `<div>` is not focusable and has no role, so it is skipped by Tab and Enter or Space can never fire its click. The tempting answer assumes it is at least reachable; it is not. Use `<button type="button">`, which is focusable and activates on Enter and Space for free.
questions.asked: The most common accessibility bug in real codebases; spotting it in a diff is a baseline expectation for a mid-level reviewer.

questions.q: Why does a screen reader user care whether you use `<main>`, `<nav>` and real `<h2>` headings rather than styled divs?
choices: Screen readers read the page in heading order rather than in source order
Tab stops on every landmark and heading, which gives keyboard users an outline
They pull up lists of landmarks and headings to jump around and skim the page
Only search engines benefit; screen readers treat divs and headings the same
questions.why: Screen readers offer shortcuts (for example H for next heading, or a landmarks menu), and surveys consistently show headings are the main way users find content. Headings and landmarks are not focusable, so Tab does not stop on them; the benefit comes through the screen reader's own navigation, not the Tab key.
questions.asked: Separates people who think semantics is SEO trivia from those who know how screen reader users actually move through a page.

questions.q: What accessible name and description does this dialog get?
questions.code:
Delete invoice?

This cannot be undone.
choices: Name "Delete invoice?", description "This cannot be undone."; `aria-label` is ignored
Name "Confirm", because `aria-label` overrides every other labelling source
Name "Confirm Delete invoice?", because both labelling attributes are joined
Name "Delete invoice?", with the paragraph read as part of that same name
questions.why: In accessible name computation `aria-labelledby` wins over `aria-label`, which wins over native labels and content. `aria-describedby` never contributes to the name; it supplies a separate description read after the name and role. Use `aria-label` only when there is no visible text to point at.
questions.asked: A precision question: getting the precedence right shows you have debugged names in the accessibility tree rather than guessing.

questions.q: An autosave shows "Draft saved" every 30 seconds. How should that status text reach screen reader users?
choices: Through `role="alert"`, because every status change should interrupt the user
Through `aria-live="assertive"`, so they hear the save straight away
By moving focus to the message, so the screen reader reads it out
Through a polite live region such as `role="status"`, read at the next pause
questions.why: A polite region queues the message until the user pauses, which suits routine confirmations. Assertive regions and `role="alert"` interrupt whatever is being read, which is right for a failed payment but hostile every 30 seconds. Moving focus yanks the user out of the field they are typing in.
questions.asked: The follow-up is usually "when would you use assertive?", and the good answer is: rarely, for time-critical errors only.

questions.q: Your click handler removes `hidden` from the panel. What else must it do?
choices: Nothing, because `aria-controls` makes the browser keep `aria-expanded` in sync
Set `aria-expanded="true"` on the button; the browser never updates it for you
Move `aria-expanded` onto the panel, because the panel is the part that expands
Add `role="dialog"` to the panel so screen readers announce that it has opened
questions.why: ARIA states are static attributes: nothing updates `aria-expanded` except your code, so a stale "collapsed" is announced after opening. `aria-controls` only records a relationship and is poorly supported, so it drives nothing. The state belongs on the control the user operates, not on the panel.
questions.asked: Tests whether you treat ARIA as state you own and keep in sync, which is where most real ARIA bugs come from.

questions.q: What is wrong with this toast?
choices: `aria-hidden` also hides it visually, so sighted users never see the toast
`aria-hidden` removes Undo from the Tab order too, so nobody can reach it with a keyboard
Undo stays focusable, so keyboard users land on a control screen readers cannot announce
Nothing, because `aria-hidden` applies only to text, not to interactive children
questions.why: `aria-hidden="true"` removes the subtree from the accessibility tree but changes neither rendering nor focus, so Tab still lands on Undo and a screen reader announces nothing useful. Never put focusable content inside `aria-hidden`; if the content really is inactive, use the `inert` attribute, which removes it from focus as well.
questions.asked: Automated tools flag this one, so the interviewer wants the mechanism: aria-hidden affects the tree, not focus or rendering.

questions.q: What does this element still lack compared with a native `<button>`?
choices: Keyboard activation: Enter and Space do nothing until you handle key events
Nothing, because `role="button"` makes the browser fire click on Enter and Space
Focusability, because `tabindex="0"` only takes effect on form controls, not divs
An accessible name, because text inside a div is never used as the button's name
questions.why: `role` changes only what assistive technology announces; it adds no behaviour. `tabindex="0"` does make the div focusable, and a button role does take its name from content, but browsers only synthesise click from Enter and Space for real buttons. You would also need disabled handling and form behaviour, which is why `<button>` is the fix.
questions.asked: Shows whether you know role is a promise to assistive technology that you must then keep in code.

questions.q: The markup order is Save, Delete, Cancel. In what order does Tab visit the buttons?
choices: Cancel, Delete, Save, because browsers follow the visual flex order
Cancel, Delete, Save, because row-reverse also reverses the tab indices
Save, Delete, Cancel on the first pass, then the visual order on every pass after that
Save, Delete, Cancel, which is DOM order and now runs right to left on screen
questions.why: Sequential focus order follows the DOM; `flex-direction`, `order`, grid placement and absolute positioning change only what you see. Focus then jumps right to left, which fails WCAG 2.4.3 Focus Order when it confuses meaning. Fix the source order rather than reordering with CSS.
questions.asked: Checks that you know CSS reordering is a keyboard bug, not just a styling choice.

questions.q: What does `tabindex="-1"` do on a heading?
choices: Removes it from the accessibility tree, so screen readers skip over the heading entirely
Makes it focusable from script with `.focus()`, but leaves it out of the Tab order
Puts it last in the Tab order, after elements with zero or positive values
Blocks focus entirely, so later `.focus()` calls on it are silently ignored
questions.why: -1 means focusable programmatically but not reachable with Tab, which is how you move focus to a heading after a route change. 0 puts an element in the natural DOM order. Positive values jump ahead of everything else and should be avoided, because they break the order for the whole page.
questions.asked: The follow-up is "why never use a positive tabindex?", and the answer is that it rewrites the order for every other element.

questions.q: Design wants no focus ring after mouse clicks, so someone wrote this. What should replace it?
choices: A visible indicator on `:focus-visible`, which typically matches keyboard focus only
Hover styles only, because keyboard users see the hover state as they Tab through the page
Nothing, because screen readers announce focus, so a visible ring is only cosmetic
An outline on `:active` only, because the ring matters only while a key is held down
questions.why: Removing the outline leaves keyboard users with no idea where they are, which fails WCAG 2.4.7 Focus Visible (AA). `:focus-visible` matches when the browser judges an indicator is needed, such as keyboard focus. Screen reader announcements do not help sighted keyboard users.
questions.asked: A code-review classic: the interviewer wants you to reject `outline: none` and offer the fix that keeps design happy.

questions.q: What is a "Skip to main content" link for, and where does it go?
choices: It sits in the footer and lets keyboard users jump back up to the page top
It is hidden from all users and read only by screen readers as a page summary
It is the first focusable element and moves focus past repeated nav to `<main>`
It is a button that collapses the navigation so that Tab reaches content sooner
questions.why: Without it a keyboard user tabs through every header and nav link on every page. It is usually visually hidden until focused, then shown. It meets WCAG 2.4.1 Bypass Blocks (Level A); landmarks help screen reader users, but sighted keyboard users still need the link.
questions.asked: Cheap to build and often missing; mentioning that it should become visible on focus is the detail interviewers look for.

questions.q: Each list row has a Delete button. After deleting row 3, the row is removed from the DOM. Where should focus go?
choices: Nowhere; the browser moves focus to the next focusable element on its own
To the page top, so the user restarts from the skip link with fresh context
Leave it; screen readers re-read the updated list, which gives enough context
To a sensible neighbour, such as the next row's Delete button, via `.focus()`
questions.why: When the focused element is removed, `document.activeElement` falls back to `<body>` and screen reader users lose their place. Nothing moves focus for you, so send it to the next row, the previous one, or the list heading when the list is empty. The same applies after an SPA route change: focus the new page's `<h1>`.
questions.asked: A production-experience signal: people who have tested their own CRUD screens with a keyboard know this bug.

questions.q: When should a required email field get `aria-invalid="true"`?
choices: On first render, because an empty required field is already invalid
After validation fails on blur or submit, removed once the value is valid
Never, because `required` already tells screen readers the field is invalid
On the submit button only, so it announces that the form contains errors
questions.why: Marking untouched fields invalid means users hear "invalid entry" before typing anything. `required` exposes the field as required, not invalid; `aria-invalid` reports a failed check, so set it when you show the error and pair it with `aria-describedby` pointing at the message.
questions.asked: Tests whether you think about what is announced over time, not just which attributes exist.

questions.q: Screen readers often say nothing when this error appears. Why?
choices: The region is inserted along with its text; it must exist before the text changes
A polite region waits for typing to stop, then drops the message after a delay

`aria-live` only takes effect on `role="alert"` elements, not on a plain `

`
Live regions announce only `textContent` writes, not DOM nodes that React inserts
questions.why: Screen readers watch existing live regions for changes; a region that arrives already containing its text is often not announced. Render the region empty from the start and change only its text. `role="alert"` is special-cased by most screen readers when inserted, which is why it seems to work where this does not.
questions.asked: A real debugging story: candidates who have tested with a screen reader know live regions must be mounted before they are used.

questions.q: A long checkout form fails validation with three errors. What does the error summary pattern add?
choices: An assertive live region that reads every error aloud while focus stays on the Submit button
A `title` tooltip on each invalid field that repeats its own error text on hover
A list of the errors at the top, focused on submit, with each linking to its field
A single `alert()` dialog that lists every error and blocks until it is dismissed
questions.why: Focusing the summary gets it read in full, tells the user how many problems there are, and each link jumps to the field, whose own message is tied to it with `aria-describedby`. An assertive region reads the list once and leaves the user to hunt; `title` tooltips are unavailable to keyboard and touch users.
questions.asked: Shows you have built forms for real users; the GOV.UK design system is the reference most interviewers have in mind.

questions.q: Why is placeholder text not a replacement for a visible `<label>`?
choices: Screen readers never read placeholders, so the field is left with no accessible name
Browsers ignore placeholders for autofill, so saved values are not suggested
Placeholders are dropped at 200% zoom, so low-vision users no longer see them
It vanishes once the user types, and default placeholder colour fails contrast
questions.why: Once the field has a value the prompt is gone, which hurts anyone who needs to check what a field wanted, especially users with memory or cognitive disabilities. Browsers do use a placeholder as a fallback accessible name, so "never read" is wrong; the problems are that it disappears and is faint.
questions.asked: Designers ask for placeholder-only forms constantly, so interviewers want to hear you can explain the cost.

questions.q: What contrast ratios does WCAG 2.2 AA require for normal body text and for large text?
choices: 3:1 for normal body text and 4.5:1 for large text
4.5:1 for normal body text and 3:1 for large text
7:1 for normal body text and 4.5:1 for large text
4.5:1 for all text, whatever its size or weight
questions.why: Criterion 1.4.3 asks 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text (24px, or about 18.7px bold). 7:1 is the AAA level. Separately, 1.4.11 asks 3:1 for UI component boundaries and focus indicators against their surroundings.
questions.asked: Knowing the numbers without looking them up signals you have actually checked a design, and the good answer mentions 3:1 for controls too.

questions.q: An orders table shows status only as a green or red dot. Which fix meets WCAG AA?
choices: Add a text label such as "Paid" or "Overdue" beside or inside each dot
Darken the red and green until each reaches 4.5:1 against the background
Add one legend above the table that explains what each colour means
Nothing, because avoiding colour-only status is an AAA requirement
questions.why: WCAG 1.4.1 Use of Colour (Level A) forbids colour as the only way to convey information. Contrast does not help a user who cannot tell red from green, and a legend still requires distinguishing the colours. Text, or an icon with an accessible name, fixes it for everyone.
questions.asked: A design-review staple; around 1 in 12 men has some colour vision deficiency, so this bug is never theoretical.

questions.q: When does the second rule apply?
choices: When the device reports low battery or has power-saving mode turned on
When a screen reader is running, since animation distracts from speech
When the browser detects that the device cannot keep up a smooth frame rate
When the user has turned on a reduce-motion setting in the OS or browser
questions.why: The media feature reflects a user preference, often set by people with vestibular disorders for whom sliding and parallax motion cause nausea. It says nothing about battery, performance or assistive technology. Keep essential feedback, for example with a fade instead of a slide.
questions.asked: Easy to support and often forgotten; the follow-up is whether reduced means none, and the answer is "less, not necessarily zero".

questions.q: An automated scanner such as axe reports zero violations on your app. What can you conclude?
choices: The app meets WCAG 2.2 AA, because the scanners test every success criterion
Only the machine-checkable rules pass; focus order and meaningful text need a manual check
The markup is valid, but you should still run the same scan across other browsers
Keyboard and screen reader behaviour pass, but contrast still needs a colour checker
questions.why: Tools can check that an image has alt text, not that the text is meaningful; that a label exists, not that it makes sense; and nothing about whether focus order or error flow is usable. Estimates put automated coverage at roughly a third to a half of issues. Contrast is actually one of the things tools check well.
questions.asked: Filters out candidates who treat a green Lighthouse score as done; the good answer describes the manual pass that follows.

questions.q: Before merging a new form, what does a five-minute manual keyboard pass check?
choices: That every element, including text and headings, receives focus in turn
That every button has a keyboard shortcut, as WCAG AA requires for forms
That every control is reachable, focus is visible, order is logical, nothing traps it
That the `tabindex` values run 1, 2, 3 and onwards to match the visual reading order
questions.why: Unplug the mouse, Tab and Shift+Tab through the form, operate every control with Enter, Space and arrows, and submit with errors to see where focus lands. Only interactive elements should be focusable, WCAG does not require shortcuts, and positive tabindex values are a bug, not a check.
questions.asked: Interviewers want a concrete habit; adding "then a quick screen reader smoke test with NVDA or VoiceOver" rounds out the answer.

questions.q: A low-vision user zooms the browser to 400%, which makes the layout 320 CSS pixels wide. What does WCAG 2.2 AA require of your orders page there?
choices: Nothing at AA; behaviour above 200% zoom is covered only by AAA criteria on visual presentation
Content reflows to one column with no horizontal scrolling, except for things like data tables
The page may disable zoom above 200% with the viewport meta tag to protect the layout
A separate mobile site is served, since desktop layouts need not support zoom
questions.why: 1.4.10 Reflow (AA) requires content to be usable at 320 CSS pixels wide without two-dimensional scrolling, which is what 400% zoom on a 1280px window produces; a mobile-first responsive layout usually passes for free. Exceptions exist for content that needs two dimensions, such as data tables and maps. Blocking zoom with `user-scalable=no` or `maximum-scale` fails 1.4.4 Resize Text and is ignored by iOS anyway.
questions.asked: Zoom users are a large group, and the question checks you connect responsive design to an actual AA criterion rather than to phones only.

questions.q: A code review shows a close button inside an off-canvas panel that has `aria-hidden="true"` while the panel is closed but still rendered. What bug does a keyboard and screen reader user hit?
choices: The links are removed from the tab order, so the drawer can never be opened
Tab still reaches the button and link, which the reader cannot describe
The browser moves `aria-hidden` onto the button, so it announces as disabled
Nothing, because `aria-hidden` also hides the content visually from everyone
questions.why: `aria-hidden` removes content from the accessibility tree but does nothing to focus or rendering, so keyboard users tab into invisible or unnamed controls: a "ghost" focus stop. Hide a closed drawer with `hidden`, `display: none` or `inert`, which remove it from both the tab order and the tree.
questions.asked: axe flags this as `aria-hidden-focus`; interviewers want you to know that ARIA changes what is announced, never what is focusable.

questions.q: A modal is open and you want everything behind it to be unreachable by Tab and invisible to screen readers. In a 2026 browser, which single attribute on the page wrapper does both?
choices: `aria-modal="true"`, placed on the wrapper element behind the dialog
`aria-hidden="true"`, which also removes descendants from the tab order
`inert`, which blocks focus, clicks and the accessibility tree together
`tabindex="-1"`, which cascades to every focusable descendant element
questions.why: `inert` (Baseline since 2023) makes a subtree non-focusable, non-clickable and hidden from assistive technology in one go. `aria-hidden` only affects the accessibility tree; `tabindex` does not cascade to children; `aria-modal` belongs on the dialog itself and only hints to screen readers. `showModal()` applies the same inertness automatically.
questions.asked: A modern-knowledge check: candidates who still hand-roll `aria-hidden` plus a focus trap have not seen `inert` or `showModal()`.

questions.q: What does a screen reader announce for this control?
choices: "Order summary" in place of the paragraph text inside the div
"Order summary, region" followed by the paragraph as a landmark
"Order summary, group" because a labelled div becomes a group
Just the paragraph; `aria-label` is ignored on a plain div
questions.why: A `<div>` has the `generic` role, and ARIA 1.2 prohibits naming generic elements, so most screen readers ignore the label entirely. Give it a role that supports a name (for example `role="region"`, or use `<section aria-labelledby>`) or make the heading visible text instead.
questions.asked: Separates people who know `aria-label` only works on elements with a role from those who sprinkle it as a comment.

questions.q: A "Bold" button in a text editor toolbar toggles formatting on and off. Which markup gives screen reader users the current state correctly?
choices: `<button aria-pressed="true">Bold</button>`, flipping the value on each click
`<button aria-selected="true">Bold</button>`, flipping the value on each click
`<button aria-checked="true">Bold</button>`, keeping the implicit button role
`<button>Bold (on)</button>`, rewriting the text between on and off each time
questions.why: `aria-pressed` turns a button into a toggle button, announced as "Bold, toggle button, pressed". `aria-selected` belongs to tabs, options and grid cells, and `aria-checked` to checkboxes, radios and switches, so on a plain button they are ignored or invalid. Rewriting the label works but loses the toggle semantics.
questions.asked: Checks that you pick the state attribute that matches the role, which is where most ARIA misuse comes from.

questions.q: A mute button's label changes from "Mute" to "Unmute" when clicked. Should it also get `aria-pressed`?
choices: Yes, because every button that changes state needs `aria-pressed` for screen readers
No, because a changing label already conveys state and "Unmute, pressed" contradicts it
Yes, but only `aria-pressed="mixed"`, as the audio might be partly muted by the OS
No, because `aria-pressed` is only valid on `<input type="checkbox">` in current ARIA
questions.why: Pick one way to express state: either a fixed label with `aria-pressed`, or a label that changes. Doing both makes a screen reader say "Unmute, toggle button, pressed", which is ambiguous about whether sound is on. `aria-pressed` is valid on buttons, and `mixed` is for tri-state toggles.
questions.asked: APG explicitly warns about this; a strong answer explains why a double signal confuses users rather than just citing the rule.

questions.q: Which attribute tells a screen reader that a link in the main navigation points at the page the user is already on?
choices: `aria-selected="true"`, the state used for the chosen item in a set
`aria-current="page"`, which is announced as "current page"
`aria-pressed="true"`, since the link is effectively switched on
`class="active"`, which screen readers expose as a selected state
questions.why: `aria-current="page"` exists for exactly this, and screen readers append "current page" to the link. `aria-selected` is not supported on links, `aria-pressed` would change the role to a toggle button, and CSS classes are invisible to assistive technology.
questions.asked: An easy one that shows whether you know that visual styling like an active class conveys nothing to a screen reader.

questions.q: A "Delete" button is disabled until a checkbox is ticked. The designer wants keyboard users to still be able to focus it and hear why it is unavailable. Which approach fits?
choices: The `disabled` attribute, since it keeps the button focusable and announced
`aria-disabled="true"` with a hint in `aria-describedby`, and a guard in the handler
`tabindex="-1"` with a greyed style, so the button is skipped until it is enabled
`aria-hidden="true"` until enabled, then remove it once the checkbox is ticked
questions.why: `disabled` removes the button from the tab order, so the user may never discover it. `aria-disabled` keeps it focusable and announced as "dimmed" or "unavailable", but it does not block clicks, so your handler must ignore activation while it is set. `aria-hidden` on a focusable control creates a ghost focus stop.
questions.asked: Interviewers use this to see whether you know `aria-disabled` is announce-only and needs a behavioural guard.

questions.q: What is the practical difference between `aria-labelledby` and `aria-describedby` on a form field?
choices: `labelledby` sets the accessible name; `describedby` adds a hint read after it
`labelledby` is read after a pause; `describedby` replaces the visible label
`labelledby` accepts one id; `describedby` is the only one that accepts several
`labelledby` is for inputs only; `describedby` works only on landmark regions
questions.why: The name is what identifies the control ("Email"); the description is supplementary ("We'll only use this for receipts") and is usually read after the name, role and state, sometimes after a pause. Both take a space-separated list of ids and work on any element that supports naming.
questions.asked: Checks you know which text belongs in the name and which in the description, which matters for voice control and verbosity.

questions.q: What is the accessible name of this input?
questions.code:
<label for="q">Search</label>
<input id="q" aria-label="Find products"
       placeholder="e.g. kettle" title="Search the catalogue">
choices: "Search", because a native `<label>` wins over every ARIA attribute
"Search the catalogue", because `title` is checked before labels
"Find products", because `aria-label` outranks the `<label>`
"e.g. kettle", because the placeholder is the text visible in the field
questions.why: Name computation checks `aria-labelledby`, then `aria-label`, then the native label, then `title` and placeholder as last resorts. So the visible "Search" is overridden, which also breaks WCAG 2.5.3 Label in Name: a voice user saying "click Search" misses. Delete the `aria-label`.
questions.asked: The name-computation order is a favourite deep question; the strong answer also spots the Label in Name failure.

questions.q: A visible label reads "Postcode", but a developer added `aria-label="Enter your ZIP or postal code here"`. Which WCAG 2.2 criterion does this fail, and who notices first?
choices: 1.4.3 Contrast, noticed first by low-vision users who zoom
2.5.3 Label in Name, noticed first by voice-control users
2.4.7 Focus Visible, noticed first by keyboard-only users
1.3.5 Input Purpose, noticed first by autofill in the browser
questions.why: 2.5.3 (Level A) requires the accessible name to contain the visible label text. A Dragon or Voice Control user says "click Postcode" and nothing matches because the name is different. Keep the visible words at the start of the name, or just drop the `aria-label`.
questions.asked: Voice control is the forgotten assistive technology; mentioning it marks you out.

questions.q: An icon-only button uses an inline SVG. Which markup gives it a clean accessible name?
choices: Add `title="Delete"` to the SVG path so the icon itself carries the name
Add `role="img"` to the SVG and leave the button text empty for brevity
Add `alt="Delete"` to the ``
Add `aria-label="Delete"` to the button and `aria-hidden="true"` to the SVG
questions.why: Naming the button and hiding the decorative SVG gives "Delete, button" with no stray graphic announcement. `alt` is not an SVG attribute, `role="img"` without a name leaves the button unnamed, and `title` on a path is unreliable across screen readers and shows a tooltip only on hover.
questions.asked: Icon buttons are in every CRUD table; interviewers expect this pattern without hesitation.

questions.q: Which `alt` value is right for a purely decorative divider image next to a heading?
choices: `alt=""`, so screen readers skip the image entirely
No `alt` attribute at all, which means decorative
`alt="decorative swirl"`, so users know to ignore it
`alt="image"`, the shortest value that passes axe
questions.why: An empty `alt` marks the image as presentational and it is dropped from the accessibility tree. Omitting `alt` entirely is a failure: many screen readers then read the file name ("swirl dot svg"). Describing decoration or saying "image" adds noise.
questions.asked: Basic, but candidates often think missing `alt` and empty `alt` are the same thing.

questions.q: An image is the only content of a link to the home page. What should its `alt` say?
choices: A description of the logo artwork, such as "blue triangle wordmark"
Empty, because the link's `href` already tells users where it goes
The destination, such as "Acme home", since it is the link's name
"Link to home page", so the role is repeated clearly for the user
questions.why: When an image is a link's only content, its `alt` becomes the link's accessible name, so it must say where the link goes. Empty `alt` leaves an unnamed link, and many screen readers then read the URL. The role is already announced, so "link to" is repeated noise.
questions.asked: Tests that you understand `alt` as a function, not a description, whenever the image does something.

questions.q: What does `role="presentation"` do to this data table, and when is it appropriate?
choices: It adds a caption role, which suits any table without a `<caption>`
It strips table semantics, so it is only right for layout tables
It hides the table from screen readers, which suits summary data
It marks the table as read-only, which suits reports and exports
questions.why: `presentation` (or `none`) removes the table, row and header semantics, so users lose "row 2, column Total" navigation and header announcements. The content is still read as plain text. It exists for legacy layout tables; a table of orders is data and must keep its semantics.
questions.asked: Shows whether you know that removing a role removes the navigation screen reader users rely on, not the content.

questions.q: A sortable orders table must tell screen reader users which column is sorted. Where does the state go?
choices: `aria-sort="ascending"` on the `<table>` element, naming the column
`aria-sort="ascending"` on the sorted column's `<th>` element only
`aria-selected="true"` on every `<td>` in the sorted table column
`aria-pressed="true"` on the header, plus an arrow icon in its text
questions.why: `aria-sort` belongs on the one column header that is currently sorted, and should be absent from the others. Put a `<button>` inside the `<th>` to make it operable. `aria-selected` on cells means cell selection in a grid, and `aria-sort` on the table is invalid.
questions.asked: Every CRUD app has a sortable table; the strong answer also mentions the button inside the header for keyboard access.

questions.q: Which CSS hides extra helper text visually while keeping it available to screen readers?
choices: `display: none`, since screen readers read the DOM rather than the page layout
`visibility: hidden`, since the element keeps its space and so stays in the tree
`opacity: 0; height: 0`, since the text remains in normal flow at zero height
`position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip-path: inset(50%)`
questions.why: The "visually hidden" pattern shrinks the element to one clipped pixel so it stays in the accessibility tree. `display: none` and `visibility: hidden` remove content from that tree. Zero height with opacity 0 is inconsistently read and can still be focused invisibly.
questions.asked: A standard utility (`sr-only` in Tailwind); interviewers check you know why `display: none` is not the same thing.

questions.q: The text that labels a field lives in an element with the `hidden` attribute. Does `aria-labelledby` pointing at it still produce a name?
questions.code: Quantity for order 1042
choices: No, hidden elements are removed from the tree, so the name is empty
Yes, `aria-labelledby` may reference hidden content to build a name
Only if the span also has `aria-hidden="false"` to re-expose its text
Only in Chromium, which is the one engine that ignores the `hidden` flag
questions.why: The accessible name algorithm follows `aria-labelledby` and `aria-describedby` references even into hidden content, by design, so authors can supply off-screen labels. The span itself is not announced as content. Prefer visible labels, but this is valid and consistent across engines.
questions.asked: A deep name-computation detail; knowing it shows you have read the spec rather than guessed from symptoms.

questions.q: What is wrong with using `role="menu"` for a website's main navigation list of links?
choices: It is fine; `menu` is the correct role for any list of links
`menu` announces an app menu expecting arrow keys and `menuitem` children
`menu` hides the links from search engines, which hurts SEO
`menu` is deprecated in ARIA 1.2 and replaced by `navigation`
questions.why: `role="menu"` promises desktop-application behaviour: arrow-key navigation, one tab stop, type-ahead and `menuitem` children. Screen readers switch to focus mode, so users who expected links get a widget that ignores their normal keys. Site navigation is `<nav>` with a list of links.
questions.asked: The single most common ARIA misuse on real sites; interviewers want you to say "use `<nav>` and links".

questions.q: A "More actions" button opens a disclosure panel of ordinary links. Which attribute pair describes it without over-promising?
choices: `aria-haspopup="menu"` and `aria-expanded`, which suit any popup panel
`aria-expanded` alone, toggled on the button, with the panel shown or hidden
`aria-haspopup="true"` alone, since expanded state is announced automatically
`aria-owns` pointing at the panel, which tells the reader that it can open
questions.why: A disclosure only needs `aria-expanded` on its button. `aria-haspopup="true"` or `"menu"` tells screen readers a `role="menu"` is coming, with arrow-key behaviour, which a panel of links does not have. `aria-owns` rewrites the tree and is not how you express open or closed.
questions.asked: Checks whether you choose the simplest accurate pattern (disclosure) over the fancy one (menu).

questions.q: When is `role="application"` justified on a region of a web page?
choices: On any single-page app root, so screen readers treat it as software
On forms with more than ten fields, so users stay in forms mode
Rarely: only for a widget like a canvas editor that handles every key itself
On navigation bars, so arrow keys move between links in the bar
questions.why: `application` turns off the screen reader's browse-mode shortcuts inside the region, passing every key to your script. That is only acceptable when you implement complete keyboard interaction and announcements yourself, such as a drawing canvas. Putting it on an app root breaks heading and landmark navigation everywhere.
questions.asked: A question about restraint; wrapping a React root in `role="application"` is a classic audit finding.

questions.q: A search results count updates after each query. Which markup announces "24 results" politely without moving focus?
choices: `role="alert"`, since the user needs to know the number straight away
`aria-live="off"`, since the region only changes after a user action
`role="status"`, rendered on load and with its text updated in place
`tabindex="0"`, so screen readers read it when the text is replaced
questions.why: `role="status"` is an implicit polite, atomic live region, so the new count is read at the next pause. The element must exist before the text changes. `alert` interrupts whatever the user is hearing, `aria-live="off"` suppresses announcements, and `tabindex` only makes it focusable.
questions.asked: Live regions are the core of 4.1.3 Status Messages; the follow-up is usually "why must it exist before the update?"

questions.q: A basket region reads "2 items, total £30" and only the number changes. Screen readers announce just "3". Which attribute makes them read the whole sentence?
choices: `aria-atomic="true"` on the live region
`aria-relevant="all"` on each of the spans
`aria-busy="false"` on the live region
`role="log"` in place of the live region
questions.why: By default a live region announces only the changed node. `aria-atomic="true"` makes the screen reader read the whole region whenever any part changes. `aria-relevant` controls which kinds of change count (additions, removals, text), `aria-busy` defers announcements, and `log` is for appended history like chat.
questions.asked: Tests whether you understand live regions beyond "add aria-live"; `role="status"` sets atomic for you.

questions.q: A data table refreshes in stages over two seconds and a live region inside it chatters through every intermediate update. What is the intended ARIA tool for this?
choices: `aria-live="assertive"`, so only the final update gets spoken
`aria-hidden="true"` on the table until all the rows have loaded
`role="alert"`, so the updates are merged into one announcement
`aria-busy="true"` while updating, set back to `false` when done
questions.why: `aria-busy="true"` tells assistive technology the region is mid-update so it can hold announcements until `aria-busy` is removed or set to false. Support varies, so also keep live regions small. `assertive` and `alert` interrupt more, not less, and `aria-hidden` hides the whole table, including rows the user may be reading.
questions.asked: Knowing `aria-busy` exists, and that support is uneven, is the kind of nuance that separates mid from senior answers.

questions.q: Your SPA shows a toast "Invoice sent" that disappears after 3 seconds. What is the accessibility problem with the 3-second timeout?
choices: None, since toasts are decorative and do not need to be accessible at all
It is too long, as WCAG requires status messages to clear within 1 second
Screen readers ignore any content that is removed within five seconds of first display
Slow readers and magnifier users may miss it; keep it longer or let them dismiss
questions.why: Magnifier users may not be looking at the toast's corner, and slow readers need time. A polite live region announces the text, but the visual message also has to last long enough (or persist until dismissed) under 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable. Never put actions only inside auto-dismissing toasts.
questions.asked: Toasts are everywhere in CRUD apps; strong candidates mention both the announcement and the timing.

questions.q: A progress bar for a CSV import is built from divs. Which markup exposes its value to assistive technology?
choices: `<div role="progressbar" aria-valuenow="40" aria-valuemin="0" aria-valuemax="100">`
`<div role="status" aria-valuenow="40" aria-valuemax="100">`, so each change is read
`<div role="slider" aria-valuenow="40">`, with its thumb styled to look like a bar
`<div aria-label="40%" class="bar">`, updated with the percentage on every tick
questions.why: `progressbar` with value attributes is the ARIA equivalent of `<progress value="40" max="100">`, which is the better choice if you can use it. `slider` implies the user can change it, `status` does not support value attributes, and a label on a generic div is ignored. Give it a name too.
questions.asked: Usually asked as "what native element would you use instead?", and the answer is `<progress>`.

questions.q: In the WAI-ARIA tabs pattern, what does the Tab key do when focus is on the active tab?
choices: Moves focus to the next tab in the tablist, wrapping round at the end
Activates the next tab and moves focus into its newly shown panel
Leaves the tablist and moves focus into the active tab's panel
Does nothing, since only the arrow keys work while inside a tablist
questions.why: A tablist is one tab stop: arrow keys move between tabs and Tab moves on to the panel (or the first focusable thing after the tablist). Making every tab a Tab stop forces keyboard users through all of them to reach the content, which is the bug the pattern exists to avoid.
questions.asked: The one-tab-stop rule for composite widgets is the heart of every keyboard-pattern question.

questions.q: Your tabs switch panels instantly with data already in memory. Which activation model does the ARIA Authoring Practices Guide recommend?
choices: Manual: arrows move focus and Enter or Space shows the panel
Automatic: moving focus with the arrows also shows the panel
Hover: the panel shows when the pointer rests on a tab label
Deferred: the panel shows after focus rests for 500 ms on a tab
questions.why: APG recommends automatic activation when panels can be displayed without noticeable latency, because it saves a keystroke per tab. Use manual activation when showing a panel triggers a slow fetch, so arrowing across five tabs does not fire five requests.
questions.asked: A good answer names both models and the latency trade-off that picks between them.

questions.q: What does a tab's markup need so a screen reader says "Invoices, tab, 2 of 4, selected"?
choices: `<a role="tab" class="active">` inside a `<nav>` element with `aria-current`
`<li role="tab" aria-expanded="true">` inside a plain `<ul>` list of tabs
`<button aria-pressed="true">` inside a `<div role="toolbar">` container
`<button role="tab" aria-selected="true">` inside a `role="tablist"` element
questions.why: Position ("2 of 4") comes from the tabs being owned by a `tablist`, and "selected" comes from `aria-selected`. Each tab should also have `aria-controls` pointing at its `role="tabpanel"`, which is labelled by the tab. `aria-expanded` is for disclosures, and `aria-pressed` makes toggle buttons.
questions.asked: Builds on the tabs question; interviewers often ask you to sketch this markup from memory.

questions.q: This roving-tabindex handler moves focus between four tabs. Which input breaks it?
choices: `nextIndex(3, 4, 'ArrowRight')`, which returns 4 and runs off the end
`nextIndex(0, 4, 'ArrowLeft')`, which returns -1, not 3
`nextIndex(2, 4, 'Home')`, which returns 2 because Home is ignored here
`nextIndex(1, 4, 'End')`, which returns 4 since `n - 1` is evaluated late
questions.why: In JavaScript `%` keeps the sign of the dividend, so `(0 - 1) % 4` is `-1` and `tabs[-1]` is undefined. Use `(i - 1 + n) % n`. ArrowRight from the last tab correctly wraps to 0, and Home and End return 0 and 3.
questions.asked: A tiny bug that ships in hand-rolled keyboard handlers; interviewers like it because it tests both JS and the pattern.

questions.q: What is "roving tabindex"?
choices: Setting `tabindex="0"` on every item so each one is reachable with Tab
Giving items rising positive `tabindex` values so Tab follows visual order
One item has `tabindex="0"` and the rest `-1`; arrows move the 0 and focus
Keeping DOM focus on the container and pointing at the item with an ARIA id
questions.why: Only the current item is in the tab sequence; the arrow-key handler sets the old item to `-1`, the new one to `0`, and calls `focus()` on it. That makes the widget a single tab stop that remembers the last item. The last option describes `aria-activedescendant`, the alternative technique.
questions.asked: Every composite widget uses this or activedescendant; interviewers ask you to name both and pick one.

questions.q: When would you choose `aria-activedescendant` over roving tabindex?
choices: When DOM focus must stay in a text input, as in a combobox
When the widget has fewer than ten items and every item can be focused
When you need the browser to scroll the active item into view for free
When the items are links that must remain in the page's Tab sequence
questions.why: With `aria-activedescendant` the container (or input) keeps real focus and the attribute names the "virtually focused" item's id, so the user can keep typing in a combobox while arrowing through suggestions. You must scroll the item into view and style it yourself, because the browser does not treat it as focused.
questions.asked: Knowing why the combobox needs activedescendant is a reliable sign of having built one.

questions.q: Per the ARIA Authoring Practices Guide, which keys open a menu button's menu and put focus on the first item?
choices: Tab or Shift+Tab, which move into the menu once it has rendered
Enter, Space or Down Arrow, focusing the first item
Only a mouse click; keyboard users use the page's shortcut keys
Right Arrow, which opens the menu the same way as in a menubar
questions.why: A menu button opens on Enter, Space or Down Arrow and moves focus to the first `menuitem` (Up Arrow may open it on the last). Inside, arrows move between items, Escape closes and returns focus to the button, and Tab closes the menu and moves on.
questions.asked: Menu buttons are the "row actions" button in every table; interviewers expect these keys.

questions.q: A row-actions menu is open and the user presses Escape. Where should focus go?
choices: To the top of the page, so the user starts again from a known point
To the first item in the table row, which is the closest landmark
Nowhere in particular; the menu closing is enough for the keyboard user
Back to the menu button that opened it, with the menu now closed
questions.why: Escape closes the menu and returns focus to its trigger, so the user continues from where they were. If focus is left on a removed menu item it falls to `<body>`, and a keyboard user has to tab from the start of the page again.
questions.asked: The same "return focus to the trigger" rule applies to dialogs, menus and popovers; interviewers check you generalise it.

questions.q: In a `role="menu"` of ten actions, the user types the letter "d". What does APG expect?
choices: Nothing, since letter keys are reserved for the screen reader's quick navigation
Focus moves to the next item whose label starts with "d", such as "Duplicate"
The item labelled "Delete" is activated immediately as a keyboard accelerator
The menu closes and the letter is typed into the page's search box instead
questions.why: Menus, listboxes and trees support type-ahead: a printable character moves focus to the next item starting with it, without activating it. Screen readers are in focus mode inside a menu, so letters reach your handler. Activating on a single letter would be a dangerous shortcut.
questions.asked: Few candidates mention type-ahead, so it is a good differentiator in a "build a menu" discussion.

questions.q: In an ARIA 1.2 combobox with a suggestions list, where does `role="combobox"` go?
choices: On a wrapping `<div>` that contains both the input and the listbox
On the `<ul>`, replacing `role="listbox"` on the suggestions list
On the `<label>`, so the name and role are announced together
On the `<input>` itself, which keeps focus while the list is open
questions.why: ARIA 1.2 moved `combobox` onto the focusable input, with `aria-controls` and `aria-expanded` describing the popup. The older ARIA 1.1 wrapper pattern was poorly supported and is now obsolete. The list keeps `role="listbox"` with `option` children.
questions.asked: Many tutorials still show the 1.1 wrapper pattern; knowing the current one shows recent, first-hand work.

questions.q: A combobox's suggestions are open and the user presses Down Arrow. With `aria-activedescendant`, what changes in the DOM?
choices: `document.activeElement` becomes the first `<li role="option">` in the list
The input's `aria-activedescendant` is set to the first option's id
The input's value is replaced by the first option's text straight away
The listbox gets `tabindex="0"` and becomes the focused element
questions.why: Focus stays in the input so typing still works; the input's `aria-activedescendant` points at the highlighted option, which you also style and mark `aria-selected="true"`. Filling the input is optional (inline autocomplete) and usually happens on Enter, not on arrowing.
questions.asked: Walks through the combobox mechanics; interviewers follow up with "and what does Escape do?"

questions.q: A user has typed "Man" in a city combobox and the list is open. What should the first press of Escape do?
choices: Close the list, keeping "Man" and focus in the input
Clear the input, close the list and move focus to the next field
Submit the form with "Man" as the typed value for the city field
Move focus back to the label so the user can hear the question
questions.why: Per APG, Escape first dismisses the popup without touching the typed text; if the list is already closed, Escape may clear the input. Clearing or moving focus on the first press throws away the user's work.
questions.asked: Escape semantics are consistent across popups; getting them right is what makes a custom widget feel native.

questions.q: Why do many teams choose a headless library such as React Aria, Radix or Ark UI for comboboxes and date pickers?
choices: They are the only way to pass an automated axe scan on complex widgets
They supply tested keyboard and ARIA behaviour; you own the styles
WCAG 2.2 requires certified components for comboboxes and date pickers
They render to canvas, which screen readers read more reliably than DOM
questions.why: A correct combobox involves dozens of keyboard, focus and announcement details that differ across screen readers. Headless libraries encode that behaviour and test it with real assistive technology, while leaving markup styling to you. axe can pass a broken hand-rolled widget, and WCAG has no certification.
questions.asked: The pragmatic answer interviewers want: build simple things by hand, use a proven library for complex widgets.

questions.q: An accordion header should be announced as a heading and be operable. Which structure is right?
choices:
`

Delivery

` with a click handler
``, so the heading sits inside the button

`
Delivery
` for styling

`

` with the panel after
questions.why: The button goes inside the heading so both semantics survive: heading navigation finds "Delivery", and the button is focusable with Enter and Space and exposes `aria-expanded`. `role="button"` on the `<h3>` erases the heading role, and headings are not allowed inside buttons.
questions.asked: Tests whether you understand that a role replaces another role, so nesting is how you keep both.

questions.q: Which HTML element gives you an accessible disclosure widget with no JavaScript?
choices: `<details>` with a `<summary>`
`<dialog>` with the `open` attribute
`<section>` with `aria-expanded`
`<menu>` with a `<li>` for each item
questions.why: `<summary>` is focusable, toggles with Enter or Space, and is announced with its expanded state. Since 2024 the `name` attribute groups several `<details>` into an exclusive accordion. `<dialog open>` is a non-modal dialog, and `<menu>` is just a list.
questions.asked: Reaching for native `<details>` before writing JS is the answer that impresses.

questions.q: A delete confirmation opens with `role="alertdialog"`. Which element should receive focus when it opens?
choices: The "Delete" button, since it is the primary action being confirmed
The dialog's heading, with `tabindex="-1"`, so the title is read first
The "Cancel" button, the least destructive way out of the dialog
The first link in the page behind it, so the user keeps their place
questions.why: APG advises focusing the least destructive control in a confirmation, so an accidental Enter does not delete. The `alertdialog` role plus `aria-describedby` makes screen readers read the message on open. For long content, focusing a static element at the top is the alternative.
questions.asked: Initial focus is a design decision; interviewers want the reasoning, not just "the first button".

questions.q: You open a native `<dialog>` with `showModal()`. Which of these do you still have to implement yourself?
choices: Closing on Escape, which native dialogs do not handle by default
Making the rest of the page inert for keyboard and screen readers
Giving the dialog an accessible name with `aria-labelledby`
Moving focus into the dialog when it opens for the first time
questions.why: `showModal()` handles focus on open, Escape (via the `cancel` event), inertness of the page behind and the top layer. It cannot invent a name: point `aria-labelledby` at the dialog's heading so screen readers announce "Delete order, dialog" rather than just "dialog".
questions.asked: Checks you know what the platform gives you and what it cannot, which is the practical `<dialog>` question.

questions.q: What is the difference between `dialog.show()` and `dialog.showModal()` for keyboard users?
choices: `show()` traps focus inside the dialog; `showModal()` does not trap it
`show()` is non-modal, so Tab can leave; `showModal()` makes the page inert
`show()` ignores Escape unless it is handled; `showModal()` ignores it too
There is none; the two differ only in whether a `::backdrop` gets painted
questions.why: `show()` opens a non-modal dialog: the rest of the page stays interactive and Escape does not close it by default. `showModal()` puts it in the top layer, makes everything else inert, closes on Escape and draws `::backdrop`. Pick based on whether the user must deal with the dialog first.
questions.asked: Many candidates know `showModal()` but not what `show()` is for; the non-modal case is a real design choice.

questions.q: A tooltip appears on hover and on keyboard focus of an info icon. Under WCAG 1.4.13 Content on Hover or Focus, which behaviour is required?
choices: The tooltip must be dismissible with Escape without moving focus or pointer
The tooltip must disappear after five seconds so that it cannot block content
The tooltip must be opened only by a click, never by hover or by focus alone
The tooltip must use the `title` attribute so every browser styles it natively
questions.why: 1.4.13 (AA) requires hover/focus content to be dismissible (Escape), hoverable (the pointer can move onto it without it vanishing) and persistent (it stays until dismissed or no longer relevant). Auto-hiding fails persistence, and the `title` tooltip fails hoverability and keyboard access.
questions.asked: Tooltips are a classic hidden failure; the three words dismissible, hoverable, persistent are what interviewers listen for.

questions.q: Where should essential information such as "Password must be 12+ characters" live, rather than only in a hover tooltip?
choices: In a `title` attribute on the input, which every screen reader reads out
In visible hint text linked to the input with `aria-describedby`
In the placeholder, which screen readers announce as the input's name
In an HTML comment beside the input, which assistive technology reads
questions.why: Touch users cannot hover and many keyboard users never trigger tooltips, so required information should be visible and programmatically linked. `aria-describedby` makes it part of the field's description. `title` is inconsistently announced and invisible on touch, and placeholders vanish while typing.
questions.asked: Checks that you design for touch and keyboard, not only for a mouse.

questions.q: A group of shipping-speed radio buttons shares `name="speed"`. How does the keyboard move between them natively?
choices: Tab moves to each radio in turn and Space selects the focused one
Tab enters the group; arrows move and check the next radio
Tab enters the group; arrows move focus and Enter confirms a choice
Only a mouse can change the choice once one of the radios is checked
questions.why: A same-named radio group is one tab stop (landing on the checked radio, or the first if none is), and arrow keys move focus and check the radio in one step. That native behaviour is what custom radio-card components must reproduce, so prefer real inputs styled with CSS.
questions.asked: Custom "radio cards" often break this; knowing the native behaviour tells you what to test.

questions.q: A kanban board lets users reorder cards by dragging. What does WCAG 2.2 require, and what fits best?
choices: Nothing, since drag and drop is an essential function exempt from WCAG
Keyboard drag with Space to lift and arrows to move is enough to comply
A single-pointer alternative, such as a "Move to…" menu on each card
A tooltip saying "drag to reorder", so the gesture is at least explained
questions.why: 2.5.7 Dragging Movements (AA) requires that anything done by dragging can also be done with single clicks or taps, which also helps tremor and switch users. Keyboard dragging helps keyboard users but does not satisfy a pointer-only user who cannot hold and drag. A "Move to…" menu serves both.
questions.asked: New in WCAG 2.2 and directly relevant to kanban-style CRUD screens.

questions.q: Your app adds single-letter shortcuts: "n" for new invoice and "d" to delete. Which WCAG criterion constrains this, and how?
choices: 2.1.1 Keyboard: every shortcut must also appear in the visible menus
2.4.3 Focus Order: shortcuts must follow the DOM order of their buttons
3.2.1 On Focus: shortcuts may only work after the page has fully loaded
2.1.4 Character Key Shortcuts: users must be able to disable or remap
questions.why: 2.1.4 (Level A) exists because speech-input users trigger single-letter shortcuts by accident when dictating. You must allow turning them off, remapping to include a modifier, or limiting them to when a component has focus. Shortcuts that use Ctrl or Alt are not affected.
questions.asked: A lesser-known criterion; bringing it up in a design discussion about shortcuts shows genuine depth.

questions.q: A list uses `aria-activedescendant` to highlight the active option, but sighted keyboard users cannot see which option is active. Why?
choices: The browser applies `:focus-visible` to the option but the CSS reset removed it
The option is not focused, so you must style it yourself, e.g. `[aria-selected=true]`
`aria-activedescendant` only works with `tabindex="-1"` on each option in the list
Screen readers draw their own highlight, which is hidden from sighted users
questions.why: Real focus stays on the container, so `:focus` and `:focus-visible` never match the option. You must add a visible style keyed to the active id or `aria-selected`, and scroll it into view. Without that, the widget fails 2.4.7 Focus Visible even though the screen reader works.
questions.asked: A subtle trade-off of activedescendant; spotting it shows you have tested with your eyes as well as a screen reader.

questions.q: A "Load more" button appends 20 rows to a list. Where should keyboard focus be after the click?
choices: On the first new row, or a heading just before it, so reading continues
Left on "Load more", which has now moved beneath the twenty new rows
On the top of the page, so the user can re-read the whole list from the start
On the browser's address bar, the default when the DOM has changed a lot
questions.why: Moving focus to the first new item (made focusable with `tabindex="-1"` if needed) lets keyboard and screen reader users continue from the new content. Leaving focus on a button that is now below the new rows forces them to navigate backwards to find what just loaded.
questions.asked: Pagination and "load more" are CRUD staples; interviewers use this to test focus-management instincts.

questions.q: A delivery form asks "Preferred day" with five radio buttons. How should the question itself be associated with the group?
choices: Wrap the radios in `<fieldset>` with the question in its `<legend>`
Put the question in an `<h3>` directly above the first radio button
Give every radio `aria-label` repeating the question before its day
Put the question in a `<label>` whose `for` names the first radio
questions.why: `<fieldset>` and `<legend>` create a named group, so screen readers announce "Preferred day, group" when entering, then each option's own label. A heading is not programmatically tied to the inputs, a `<label>` can only label one control, and repeating the question in every name is verbose.
questions.asked: Radio groups without a legend are among the commonest form failures in audits.

questions.q: Which attribute lets browsers and password managers autofill a user's email, and satisfies WCAG 1.3.5 Identify Input Purpose?
choices: `name="email"`, since autofill keys on the field's submitted name
`inputmode="email"`, which tells the browser what the value means
`autocomplete="email"`, one of the standard input-purpose tokens
`aria-label="email"`, which exposes the purpose to assistive tech
questions.why: `autocomplete` tokens such as `email`, `given-name`, `street-address` and `one-time-code` declare what the field collects, which drives autofill and lets assistive tools add familiar icons. `inputmode` only picks a virtual keyboard, and `name` heuristics are unreliable.
questions.asked: Autofill helps motor and cognitive disabilities as much as convenience; the token list is worth knowing.

questions.q: The login form blocks paste in the password field "for security". Which WCAG 2.2 criterion does that undermine?
choices: 3.3.7 Redundant Entry, because the password must be typed twice
3.3.8 Accessible Authentication, since it stops password managers
2.1.1 Keyboard, because Ctrl+V is a keyboard shortcut in the field
1.4.3 Contrast, since the masked dots fail the minimum contrast
questions.why: 3.3.8 (AA, new in 2.2) says login must not rely on a cognitive function test such as recalling a password unless there is help, and allowing paste and password managers is that help. Blocking paste adds no real security and forces memorisation and retyping.
questions.asked: A WCAG 2.2 addition that touches every auth screen; also a chance to show you know blocking paste is security theatre.

questions.q: A checkout asks for the billing address after the user already entered a delivery address. What does WCAG 2.2 criterion 3.3.7 Redundant Entry expect?
choices: Pre-fill it, or offer "Same as delivery address"
Hide the billing address step completely for keyboard-only users
Require the user to type it again to confirm it is still accurate
Show the delivery address as placeholder text in the billing fields
questions.why: Within one process, information the user already gave must be auto-populated or selectable, unless re-entry is essential (such as confirming a new password). That helps users with memory or motor impairments. Placeholder text is not an entered value and disappears as they type.
questions.asked: Maps directly to real checkout and onboarding flows; interviewers like candidates who know the 2.2 additions.

questions.q: A form validates each field on every keystroke and shows "Invalid email" as soon as the user types the first letter. What is the better timing?
choices: Validate only on submit, never during entry, to avoid all interruptions
Validate on every keystroke, but announce errors with `role="alert"`
Validate on blur, or on submit, then re-check on input once shown
Validate every two seconds on a timer while the field has focus
questions.why: Showing an error before the user has finished typing is noise, and with a live region it interrupts a screen reader user on every key. Validate when they leave the field or submit; once an error is showing, re-validate as they type so it clears promptly. Submit-only works but gives late feedback on long forms.
questions.asked: Validation timing is a UX and accessibility question at once; the "reward early, punish late" answer is what interviewers want.

questions.q: Which error message best meets WCAG 3.3.3 Error Suggestion for a date field?
choices: "Invalid input." shown in red text under the date field
"Error 422: validation failed" shown at the top of the page
A red border around the date field, with no text alongside it
"Enter the date as DD/MM/YYYY, for example 07/03/2026."
questions.why: 3.3.3 (AA) asks that, when you know how to fix an error, you say so. Naming the expected format with an example tells users how to recover. A generic message or status code does not, and a border alone also fails 1.4.1 Use of Colour.
questions.asked: Error copy is part of accessibility; interviewers often ask you to rewrite a bad message on the spot.

questions.q: A required field is marked only with a red asterisk. What does a screen reader user miss, and what is the fix?
choices: Nothing; screen readers announce red text as "required" by convention
It hears "star" but the field is not flagged; add `required`
The label is lost entirely; move the asterisk into the placeholder text
The asterisk is fine, but the input needs `aria-invalid="true"` from load
questions.why: Colour means nothing to a screen reader, and "star" may or may not be understood. `required` (or `aria-required="true"`) makes the field announce "required". Explain the asterisk at the top of the form for sighted users, and never set `aria-invalid` before the user has tried.
questions.asked: Basic but frequently wrong in production forms; shows whether you think in terms of what is programmatically exposed.

questions.q: A field shows an error below it after a failed submit. Which pair of attributes connects them so the error is read with the field?
questions.code: Quantity must be at least 1
choices: `aria-invalid="true" aria-describedby="qty-err"`
`aria-invalid="true" aria-labelledby="qty-err"`
`aria-live="polite" aria-controls="qty-err"`
`required aria-owns="qty-err"` on the text input
questions.why: `aria-invalid` sets the "invalid entry" state and `aria-describedby` makes the message the field's description, so focusing it reads "Quantity, invalid entry, Quantity must be at least 1". Using `aria-labelledby` would replace the field's name with the error text.
questions.asked: The core error wiring; the follow-up is often "what about `aria-errormessage`?"

questions.q: Why do many teams still use `aria-describedby` rather than `aria-errormessage` for field errors in 2026?
choices: `aria-errormessage` was removed from ARIA 1.2 and is now invalid
`aria-errormessage` only works on `<form>`, not individual inputs
Screen reader support for `aria-errormessage` is still uneven
`aria-describedby` is required by WCAG, and the other one is AAA
questions.why: `aria-errormessage` is valid ARIA and is exposed only while `aria-invalid="true"`, which is elegant, but support across screen reader and browser pairs has lagged. `aria-describedby` works everywhere. WCAG does not mandate either attribute.
questions.asked: Shows you choose attributes by real support, not by what the spec says should work.

questions.q: A form submission fails server-side with a 422 and three field errors. What should the client do for keyboard and screen reader users?
choices: Show each error by its field and leave focus on the submit button
Show the errors, then focus the first bad field or a summary
Show a native `alert()` listing all errors, then reload the form empty
Show the errors as a toast that vanishes after four seconds on screen
questions.why: Mapping the 422 body back to fields is half the job; the other half is moving focus so the user hears and reaches the problem. Leaving focus on the button means a screen reader user hears nothing. Clearing the form or hiding errors in a timed toast destroys their work or the information.
questions.asked: Joins the API side (RFC 9457 problem details) with the UI side; fullstack interviewers like that link.

questions.q: A session times out after 15 minutes and the user loses their half-finished form. What does WCAG 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable require?
choices: Nothing, since security-driven timeouts are always exempt from WCAG
The timeout must be at least 60 minutes on any form that has fields
The form must save to `localStorage` on every keystroke as a backup
Warn before expiry and let the user extend with a simple action
questions.why: 2.2.1 (Level A) requires that users can turn off, adjust or extend a time limit, typically by a warning with at least 20 seconds to press "Stay signed in". There are exceptions for real-time events and limits over 20 hours, but not a blanket security exemption.
questions.asked: Session timeouts are a backend decision with an accessibility cost; interviewers like candidates who connect the two.

questions.q: Changing a "Sort by" `<select>` immediately reloads the page with the new order. Which WCAG criterion does this risk failing?
choices: 3.2.2 On Input: changing a setting causes a context change
2.4.4 Link Purpose, because the options do not describe their destinations
1.3.1 Info and Relationships, because the select has no visible legend
2.5.8 Target Size, because native option lists render below 24 pixels
questions.why: Keyboard users arrow through options, and each arrow press changes the value, so a navigate-on-change select can reload before they reach the option they want. Either add an Apply button or warn users beforehand. Re-sorting in place without navigating or moving focus is fine.
questions.asked: A classic auto-submit bug; interviewers ask it to see if you think about keyboard users arrowing through options.

questions.q: A link colour inside paragraphs is distinguishable from body text only by hue, with no underline. What does WCAG require?
choices: Nothing, because links are exempt from 1.4.1 Use of Colour
A 4.5:1 contrast between the link text and the page background
An underline, or 3:1 contrast with text plus a hover/focus cue
A `title` attribute on each link so the difference is announced
questions.why: Under 1.4.1, colour alone cannot mark a link in a block of text. Underlines are the simple fix. The documented alternative is 3:1 contrast between link and surrounding text plus a non-colour cue on hover and focus. Links in navigation bars are identifiable by position, so this is about inline links.
questions.asked: Designers often remove underlines; interviewers want you to know the rule and the negotiated alternative.

questions.q: What minimum contrast does WCAG 2.2 AA require for a text input's border against the page background?
choices: 4.5:1, the same as the body text inside the input
7:1, because form controls fall under the AAA rule
No minimum, as borders are decorative in WCAG
3:1, under 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast
questions.why: 1.4.11 requires 3:1 for visual information needed to identify a component and its states, such as input borders, checkbox outlines, icons and focus indicators. Pale grey borders on white often fail. Text inside the input still needs 4.5:1.
questions.asked: Light grey form borders are a design-system staple that often fails; knowing 1.4.11 lets you push back with the rule.

questions.q: Which of these is exempt from WCAG 1.4.3 contrast requirements?
choices: Placeholder text that tells the user the expected format
Text on a disabled button that cannot currently be used
Error text shown in red under an invalid form field
Text in a table footer summing the order totals
questions.why: Text in inactive (disabled) components, pure decoration and logos are exempt. Placeholder text still conveys information, so it needs 4.5:1, which is one reason pale placeholders fail. Error and footer text are ordinary content.
questions.asked: Designers ask this constantly; knowing the exemptions stops pointless arguments about greyed-out buttons.

questions.q: White text sits on a hero photo. Contrast varies from 9:1 over the dark sky to 2:1 over the beach. How do you make it pass reliably?
choices: Measure the average colour of the photo and check against that
Add a text shadow, which contrast tools always count as passing
Add a semi-opaque dark overlay or backing box behind the text
Pass it, since text over images is exempt from contrast checks
questions.why: Contrast is judged against the actual pixels behind every part of the text, so the worst area counts, not the average. A scrim or solid backing guarantees the ratio as images change. Text over images is not exempt, and a thin shadow may help but is hard to verify.
questions.asked: Marketing pages break this constantly; the strong answer mentions the worst-case pixels and a guaranteed backing.

questions.q: How do you honour a user's OS setting to reduce motion for a page-transition animation?
choices: `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { .page { animation: fade 200ms; } }`
`@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { .page { animation: none; } }` for night
`@media (hover: none) { .page { animation: none; } }`, to target touch devices
`@media (max-width: 600px) { .page { animation: none; } }`, for small screens
questions.why: `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` reflects the OS "reduce motion" setting used by people with vestibular disorders. Swap movement for a gentle fade rather than removing all feedback. Colour scheme, hover capability and width say nothing about motion sensitivity.
questions.asked: The follow-up is usually "and in JavaScript?", where the answer is `matchMedia` with the same query.

questions.q: A scroll-to-top button uses `window.scrollTo({ top: 0, behavior: 'smooth' })`. How do you respect reduced motion in JavaScript?
choices: Check `navigator.reducedMotion`, which returns true when the OS setting is on
Read `matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches` then `'auto'`
Wrap the call in `requestAnimationFrame`, which skips animation automatically
Nothing: browsers ignore `behavior: 'smooth'` when the OS setting is enabled
questions.why: Scripts see the setting through `matchMedia`, and can listen for its `change` event. `navigator.reducedMotion` does not exist, and browsers do not reliably drop smooth scrolling for you in script calls. Also guard CSS `scroll-behavior: smooth` behind the media query.
questions.asked: Shows you can apply the preference in both CSS and JS, which JS-heavy animation libraries need.

questions.q: A promo carousel auto-advances every 4 seconds and loops forever. What does WCAG 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide require?
choices: A visible way to pause or stop it, as it moves for over 5 seconds
Nothing, as long as each slide stays visible for at least 3 seconds
Moving it into an `aria-live="assertive"` region so changes are heard
Disabling the carousel on mobile screens, where it is hardest to read
questions.why: Content that moves automatically, lasts more than five seconds and sits alongside other content needs a pause, stop or hide mechanism. A live region on a rotating carousel makes things worse by announcing every slide. Pausing on hover and focus is good practice, but a visible pause button is what satisfies the criterion.
questions.asked: Carousels are a perennial audit finding; the live-region distractor catches people who over-apply ARIA.

questions.q: In Windows forced colours (high contrast) mode, a button's custom focus style `box-shadow: 0 0 0 3px #4a90e2` disappears. What fixes it?
choices: Add `!important` to the box-shadow so the forced palette cannot override it
Also set `outline: 2px solid transparent`, which forced colours repaint
Swap the box-shadow for a `background-image` gradient ring round the button
Nothing; forced colours mode users are expected to rely on the caret instead
questions.why: Forced colours mode removes box-shadows and replaces author colours with the user's palette, but it keeps outlines and recolours them, so a transparent outline becomes a visible ring. `!important` does not beat forced colours, and background images behind text are dropped.
questions.asked: Forced colours is where many design systems fail silently; the transparent-outline trick is a known senior tell.

questions.q: Which media query lets you adjust styles specifically for Windows high contrast and other forced palettes?
choices: `@media (prefers-contrast: more)`
`@media (forced-colors: active)`
`@media (inverted-colors: inverted)`
`@media (color-gamut: srgb)` for low gamut
questions.why: `forced-colors: active` matches when the user agent enforces a limited palette, and you can use system colours such as `CanvasText` and `Highlight` inside it. `prefers-contrast: more` is a softer preference that does not force colours. Use `forced-color-adjust: none` only for things like colour swatches.
questions.asked: Distinguishing `prefers-contrast` from `forced-colors` shows real exposure to high-contrast testing.

questions.q: A sticky footer bar covers the bottom 80px of the viewport, so tabbing to a link near the bottom hides it completely behind the bar. Which WCAG 2.2 AA criterion fails, and what is a CSS fix?
choices: 2.4.7 Focus Visible; add `outline-offset: 80px` to push the ring clear
