1.4.10 Reflow; replace the bar with a hamburger menu on small screens
2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum); add `scroll-padding-bottom: 80px`
2.4.3 Focus Order; set a positive `tabindex` on the footer bar controls
questions.why: 2.4.11 (new in 2.2) requires a focused element not to be entirely hidden by author content such as sticky headers, footers or cookie banners. `scroll-padding` on the scroll container makes the browser scroll focused elements clear of the bar. Positive tabindex breaks focus order.
questions.asked: Sticky headers and cookie banners are everywhere; knowing `scroll-padding` turns an audit finding into a one-line fix.

questions.q: A row of 16×16px icon buttons sits in a dense table toolbar. What does WCAG 2.2 criterion 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) require?
choices: Targets at least 44×44 CSS px with no exceptions for tables
Targets at least 24×24 CSS px, or spaced well enough apart
Targets at least 16×16 CSS px, which these icon buttons meet
Targets of any size, provided that a tooltip names each icon
questions.why: 2.5.8 (AA) sets 24×24 CSS pixels, with an exception if a 24px circle centred on each target does not overlap another target, plus exceptions for inline links and equivalents. 44×44 is the AAA criterion 2.5.5 and a platform guideline. Padding the buttons is usually the easiest fix.
questions.asked: Commonly asked since 2.2; many candidates still quote 44px as the AA rule.

questions.q: A SPA route change swaps the main content but the tab still reads "Dashboard | Acme". What is the accessibility problem?
choices: Nothing; titles only matter for search engines, not for people
Screen readers use the title to set the page's language and voice
The browser blocks history navigation until the title is updated
Users hear the stale title and cannot tell which page they are on
questions.why: 2.4.2 Page Titled covers each view: screen readers announce the title on navigation, and users with many tabs rely on it. Set `document.title` on every route change alongside moving focus to the new `<h1>`. Language comes from `lang`, not the title.
questions.asked: Framework routers often forget this; interviewers pair it with the "where does focus go on route change?" question.

questions.q: A British English site includes a paragraph quoted in French. What markup makes screen readers pronounce both correctly?
choices: `<meta charset="fr">` in the head, and no attribute on the blockquote
`translate="no"` on the blockquote so it is kept in the original text
`<html lang="en-GB">` on the root, and `lang="fr"` on the blockquote
`dir="fr"` on the blockquote so the reader knows to switch its accent
questions.why: `lang` on `<html>` meets 3.1.1 Language of Page (A), and `lang` on a passage meets 3.1.2 Language of Parts (AA), letting the screen reader switch voice. `charset` is encoding, `dir` is text direction, and `translate` only stops translation tools.
questions.asked: A missing `lang` makes a screen reader read English with the wrong voice; it is one of axe's most common findings.

questions.q: You develop on Windows and want a free screen reader for a quick smoke test. Which pairing reflects how real users commonly run it?
choices: JAWS with Safari, the combination most screen reader users rely on
VoiceOver with Edge, which ships with Windows 11 out of the box
TalkBack with Firefox, the default reader for desktop Windows
NVDA with Chrome or Firefox, both widely used with it in surveys
questions.why: NVDA is free, open source and one of the most used desktop screen readers, typically with Chrome or Firefox. JAWS is commercial and Windows-only (usually with Chrome), VoiceOver is Apple's and pairs with Safari, TalkBack is Android's. Windows' built-in reader is Narrator, best with Edge.
questions.asked: Interviewers check you know which reader goes with which browser, because bugs are often pair-specific.

questions.q: In NVDA's browse mode, what does pressing the H key do?
choices: Jumps to the next heading on the page
Types "h" into the currently focused input
Opens NVDA's help for the current element
Hides the current element from the reader
questions.why: In browse mode single letters are quick-navigation keys: H for headings, D for landmarks, K for links, F for form fields, T for tables. That is why a sensible heading structure matters so much. In focus mode (inside an input) letters go to the page instead.
questions.asked: Knowing how screen reader users actually move around explains why headings and landmarks matter.

questions.q: Your custom listbox handles ArrowDown in a `keydown` listener. With NVDA in browse mode, pressing Down Arrow reads the next line of text instead. Why?
choices: NVDA disables JavaScript `keydown` listeners on every web page
`keydown` does not fire for arrow keys in Chromium-based browsers
Browse mode eats arrows; a widget role switches it to focus mode
The listener must be registered on `window`, not on the listbox element
questions.why: In browse mode the screen reader intercepts keys for its own virtual cursor. Focusing an element with a widget role such as `listbox`, `menu`, `grid` or `tablist` makes NVDA and JAWS switch to focus (forms) mode and pass arrows through. A styled `<div>` with no role never triggers that switch.
questions.asked: Explains the "works with keyboard, broken with screen reader" bug that puzzles many developers.

questions.q: Where in Chrome DevTools do you check the computed accessible name and role of an element?
choices: Elements panel, its Accessibility sidebar pane
Network panel, the Headers tab of the page request
Application panel, the Frames section for the page
Performance panel, the Interactions track at the top
questions.why: The Accessibility pane shows the element's computed name, role, states and where the name came from, and can switch the Elements tree to a full accessibility tree view. Firefox has a dedicated Accessibility Inspector with similar data and colour-deficiency simulation.
questions.asked: Checking the computed name is faster than launching a screen reader for most naming bugs.

questions.q: On macOS, what is the VoiceOver rotor useful for during a quick developer test?
choices: Changing the speech rate while a page is being read aloud to you
Listing headings, links, landmarks and form controls to spot gaps
Recording a transcript of everything VoiceOver said for the report
Emulating TalkBack so that one test covers Android devices as well
questions.why: The rotor (VO+U) lists page elements by type, which is how many users skim. A heading list with "Untitled" entries or links all called "Edit" shows problems in seconds. It changes neither speech output logging nor emulates other readers.
questions.asked: Describing a two-minute rotor check shows you actually test with VoiceOver, not just read about it.

questions.q: A table has twenty rows each with a link reading "Edit". What does a screen reader user hear in a list of links, and what is the fix?
choices: Twenty "Edit" links; add visually hidden context such as "Edit order 1042"
The row text, since links in tables are named from their row automatically
Nothing, as links inside tables are never listed in link navigation lists
Twenty "Edit" links; rename them "Click here to edit" so they are clearer
questions.why: Link and button lists strip context, so twenty identical names are useless. Add hidden context ("Edit order 1042") or `aria-labelledby` pointing at the button and the row's key cell. "Click here" adds words without meaning.
questions.asked: Identical row actions are in every CRUD table; this is 2.4.4 Link Purpose applied to real screens.

questions.q: Headings on a settings page go `h1` → `h4` → `h2` because the designer liked the h4 size. What is the problem?
choices: Browsers refuse to render an `h4` that follows an `h1` element
Search engines drop pages that have headings out of numeric order
Level is structure; size it with CSS and keep the outline
None; screen readers ignore heading levels and only list the text
questions.why: Screen reader users navigate by heading level, and skipped or inverted levels suggest missing or misplaced sections. Choose the level from the outline, then style it with a class. Browsers render any order, and the SEO effect is negligible.
questions.asked: Tests the separation of structure from presentation, which runs through all accessibility work.

questions.q: A complex data table has two header rows. What makes each data cell announce the right headers?
choices: `<th scope>` for simple headers; `id` plus `headers` for complex ones
`role="grid"` on the table so screen readers compute headers from the layout
`aria-label` on every `<td>` repeating its column and row header names in full
Bold text in the first row, which screen readers treat as a header row
questions.why: `scope` handles simple row and column headers; for multi-level headers, `headers="id1 id2"` on each cell lists exactly which headers apply. `role="grid"` adds interactive keyboard expectations without fixing associations, and bold styling conveys nothing to assistive technology.
questions.asked: Reports and dashboards produce complex tables; knowing `headers` shows depth beyond basic `<th>`.

questions.q: An embedded map is an `<iframe>` with no attributes other than `src`. What does a screen reader announce when reaching it?
choices: "Map, frame", since browsers infer a name from the embedded URL
Nothing; screen readers never enter iframes, so a name is optional
"Frame", or the embedded page's title; give it a `title`
The alt text of the map image, which the frame passes up to the page
questions.why: An iframe needs an accessible name, conventionally `title="Store locations map"`, so users know what the frame contains before entering it. Screen readers do enter frames. Without a title the announcement is vague or depends on the embedded document.
questions.asked: Embeds (maps, payment fields, videos) are common in CRUD apps and axe flags unnamed frames constantly.

questions.q: A product video has speech and no captions. Which WCAG AA requirements apply to pre-recorded video with audio?
choices: A transcript alone, which covers every requirement for video
Captions, plus audio description where visuals carry meaning
Nothing, provided the page has a text summary of the video
Sign language interpretation in a corner of every video frame
questions.why: 1.2.2 Captions (A) and 1.2.5 Audio Description (AA) apply to pre-recorded synchronised media; a transcript can stand in for audio description only at Level A. Sign language is AAA. Use `<track kind="captions">` with WebVTT for captions.
questions.asked: Media rules are a common gap; knowing captions and audio description are separate things is the key point.

questions.q: What does axe's "incomplete" (needs review) result category mean in an automated test run?
choices: The rule crashed, so the results for that page cannot be trusted
The rule found something it cannot decide, and a human must check it
The rule was skipped because it only applies to WCAG AAA criteria
The rule passed on some elements, so the page is partially compliant
questions.why: axe returns `violations`, `passes`, `inapplicable` and `incomplete`. Incomplete means it could not determine the outcome, for example contrast over a background image or gradient. Failing only on `violations` is standard, but someone should review incomplete items.
questions.asked: Shows you have read axe's output rather than just a green tick.

questions.q: You run axe with jest-axe or vitest-axe on a component rendered in jsdom. Which class of issue can it not detect there?
choices: Missing form labels, since jsdom does not model the label element
Invalid ARIA attributes, since jsdom strips unknown attributes
Missing `alt` on images, since jsdom never loads the image files
Colour contrast, since jsdom does no layout or rendering at all
questions.why: jsdom has no layout engine, so it cannot compute rendered colours, sizes or overlap; the contrast rule is disabled or unreliable there. Labels, ARIA validity and `alt` are DOM checks that work fine. Run axe in a real browser (Playwright) for contrast and layout-dependent rules.
questions.asked: Tells the interviewer you know which layer each test belongs in, not just that "we run axe".

questions.q: An end-to-end test runs axe with Playwright on the orders page as it first loads. Which bug is it most likely to miss?
choices: A missing `lang` attribute on the page's root `<html>` element
An unlabelled input in a delete dialog that is closed on load
Low contrast on the table's body text, visible when the page loads
Duplicate `id` values on elements rendered in the initial page
questions.why: axe only scans the DOM that exists when you call it, so closed dialogs, menus and error states are never checked. Drive the UI into each state (open the dialog, submit an invalid form) and run the scan again. The other issues are all present on load.
questions.asked: The practical follow-up to "we run axe in CI": which states do you scan?

questions.q: A team wants axe in CI to check WCAG 2.2 AA only. Which configuration of `@axe-core/playwright`'s `AxeBuilder` expresses that?
choices: `.withRules(['wcag22aa'])`, since rules and tags are the same identifiers
`.options({ level: 'AA' })`, the built-in conformance level switch
`.withTags(['wcag2a','wcag2aa','wcag21a','wcag21aa','wcag22aa'])`
`.include('wcag22aa')`, which filters rules by their WCAG version
questions.why: axe tags rules by standard and level, and each WCAG version's tag only covers criteria new in that version, so AA conformance to 2.2 needs the A and AA tags of 2.0, 2.1 and 2.2. `include` takes CSS selectors for page regions, and `withRules` takes rule ids such as `color-contrast`.
questions.asked: Getting the tag list right is a detail that shows hands-on set-up rather than copy-paste.

questions.q: A third-party chat widget causes axe violations you cannot fix. What is the responsible way to keep your CI check useful?
choices: Disable axe in CI until the vendor fixes the widget in a future release
Exclude the widget's container and log the issue with the vendor
Set the test to pass whenever the violation count stays below twenty
Remove `aria-*` attributes from the widget at runtime to silence the rules
questions.why: `.exclude('#chat-widget')` keeps the rest of the page gated, and the known gap is tracked instead of hidden. Disabling the whole check lets your own regressions through, a count threshold hides new bugs behind old ones, and stripping ARIA usually makes the widget worse.
questions.asked: A realistic trade-off question; interviewers want scoped exceptions, not an off switch.

questions.q: Your team adds `eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y`. Which bug can a lint rule catch that a runtime scan might miss?
choices: A `<div onClick>` with no key handler or role, anywhere in source
Text over a photo whose contrast falls below 4.5:1 on some screens
Focus that lands behind a sticky footer when the user presses Tab
A live region that is inserted at the same time as its message
questions.why: Static analysis sees every component in the codebase, including states and pages no test renders, so it catches patterns like click handlers on non-interactive elements. It cannot see rendered colours, layout or timing, which is what the other three need.
questions.asked: Checks that you think of lint, component tests, E2E scans and manual testing as layers with different reach.

questions.q: A Testing Library test calls `screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save order' })` and it fails, though a Save button is visible. What does that usually tell you?
choices: The test needs `getByText`, since role queries only find native buttons
The button's accessible name differs, or it lacks a button role
The button is rendered in a portal, which role queries cannot reach
Role queries ignore buttons until `userEvent.setup()` has been called
questions.why: `getByRole` queries the accessibility tree, so a failure often means an icon-only button with no name, a `<div>` with no role, or a name that differs from the visible text. Switching to `getByText` hides the bug. Portals render into `document.body`, which `screen` covers.
questions.asked: Role-based queries are free accessibility tests; interviewers like candidates who treat a failing query as a finding.

questions.q: Playwright can snapshot a page region's accessibility tree with `toMatchAriaSnapshot`. What kind of regression does that guard against?
choices: Pixel-level visual changes in fonts, colours and spacing
Slower page loads caused by extra JavaScript in the bundle
Changed roles, names or structure, such as a lost heading
Server errors on API calls made while the page is loading
questions.why: An ARIA snapshot records roles and names in a YAML-like tree, so a refactor that turns a button into a div or drops a heading shows up as a diff. It is not a screenshot test and says nothing about speed or network errors.
questions.asked: A 2025-era Playwright feature; mentioning it shows you keep up with accessibility tooling.

questions.q: A Lighthouse accessibility score of 100 is posted in the team channel as proof the app is accessible. What is the accurate response?
choices: It proves WCAG 2.2 AA conformance for every page that was scanned
It proves Level A conformance, and AA needs a separate audit on top
It means no tested rule failed, which is a subset of what WCAG needs
It is meaningless, since Lighthouse does not run any accessibility rules
questions.why: Lighthouse runs a weighted subset of axe rules on one page state. A perfect score means none of those failed; it cannot judge keyboard flows, focus order, meaningful alt text or whether errors make sense. It is useful, just not a conformance claim.
questions.asked: A common misunderstanding; the strong answer names specific things only a human can check.

questions.q: What does a sensible accessibility test pyramid for a React CRUD app look like?
choices: Only manual audits once a year by an external accessibility vendor
Only Lighthouse in CI, failing the build below a score of 90
Only screen reader tests, recorded and replayed in the pipeline
Lint, then axe in component and E2E tests, then manual key-flow passes
questions.why: Each layer catches different things: lint finds patterns early, axe catches rule violations in rendered states, and manual keyboard and screen reader passes catch usability that no tool understands. Annual audits alone find problems months late. Automated screen reader replay is not a mainstream practice.
questions.asked: Interviewers use this open question to hear whether you have an actual process.

questions.q: A screen reader announces "clickable" on a `<div>` that has a click handler and nothing else. What does that tell you?
choices: The div is accessible, because the reader has found and announced it
It saw a listener, but there is no role, name or keyboard access
The div is focusable, because a click handler adds it to the Tab order
The div has `role="button"` added automatically by the browser engine
questions.why: Some readers expose "clickable" from the presence of a listener, which helps a little in browse mode, but the element has no role, is not in the Tab order and does not respond to Enter or Space. Use a `<button>`.
questions.asked: Tests whether you treat "it announces something" as success, which is a common false positive in manual tests.

questions.q: A heading uses `text-transform: uppercase` in CSS versus typing "ORDER HISTORY" in capitals in the HTML. Why prefer the CSS?
choices: Some screen readers spell typed capitals out, like an acronym
CSS uppercase text meets higher contrast ratios than the typed capitals
Typed capitals fail the WCAG 2.2 rule that bans all-caps body content
Search engines ignore any heading text that has been typed in capitals
questions.why: Screen readers read the DOM text, so typed "ORDER" may be read letter by letter or with odd emphasis in some reader and voice combinations, while CSS changes only the rendering. It also makes copy easier to change. WCAG has no all-caps rule.
questions.asked: A small detail that shows you understand screen readers read source text, not pixels.

questions.q: In Safari with VoiceOver, a `<ul>` styled with `list-style: none` is no longer announced as a list. What is the usual fix?
choices: Replace the list with `<div>` elements, since lists add no information
Add `role="list"` to the `<ul>` to restore list semantics explicitly
Add `aria-live` to the list so each item is announced when it appears
Set `display: list-item` on each `<li>` with the markers hidden in CSS
questions.why: WebKit deliberately drops list semantics from unstyled lists in many contexts, reasoning that not every styled list is meaningful. Adding `role="list"` restores "list, 5 items" where the grouping matters, such as a product grid. It is a known redundant-looking role that is actually needed.
questions.asked: A known WebKit quirk; it explains a redundant-looking `role="list"` in code review.

questions.q: What does a five-minute screen reader smoke test of a new "Create invoice" form cover, as a developer rather than a specialist?
choices: Checking colour contrast of every label with the screen reader running
Checking the page renders identically in NVDA, JAWS and VoiceOver
Tab through, listen for each name, role, state and error, then submit
Checking that every paragraph is read at the default speech speed
questions.why: The fast, high-value check is whether every control has a sensible name and role, required and invalid states are announced, and errors and success messages are heard after submit. Screen readers do not measure contrast, and full cross-reader testing is a specialist audit.
questions.asked: Interviewers want to hear a concrete, repeatable routine rather than "we test with screen readers".

questions.q: A loading spinner shows while an orders table fetches. What should screen reader users get?
choices: The spinner SVG's `alt` text, read every time the animation loops
Nothing, since loading states are purely visual and brief by nature
A `role="alert"` saying "Loading" each time a request is made
A polite status such as "Loading orders", then "24 orders loaded"
questions.why: A persistent `role="status"` region can announce the start and the result so users know something happened and when it finished. `alert` is too aggressive for routine loading, and an animated icon has nothing meaningful to repeat. Keep messages brief to avoid chatter on fast loads.
questions.asked: Loading states are in every CRUD screen; the answer shows whether you think about what silence means to a blind user.
